decry

/dih-KRY/ - rhymes with deny · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Decry means to criticize openly.

Every generation of grandparents finds something new to decry — this year it is wireless earbuds at the dinner table.

Example

The transit app's update dropped the night map, and the city's night shift wasted no time: hundreds of nurses and warehouse crews flooded the developer's message boards and the morning call-in shows to decry an update that treated riders asleep by midnight as the only riders who mattered.

Decry is the exact word because the criticism is open and aimed at a practice: the workers raise a public cry against the update itself. Grumbling in a break room would be private; mourning the old map would be mere sadness. To decry is to say out loud, where everyone can hear, that a thing deserves disapproval — and to keep saying it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

criticize: To criticize is the plain, all-purpose word for finding fault, in any setting and at any volume — a margin note criticizes as quietly as a protest sign shouts. Decry narrows it: the fault-finding is public and raised-voice, aimed at a practice, and kept up where everyone can hear.

bemoan: To bemoan something is to voice sorrow over it — hands wrung, the loss mourned aloud — with blame a distant second or missing entirely. Decry runs the other way: blame first, raised in public against a target that has earned the disapproval.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

applaud: to voice open approval

praise: to speak well of something, in public or in private

Where it sits · how openly the complaint is voiced

grumble → decry → revile

grumble vs. decry: To grumble is to mutter your discontent under your breath; to decry is to lift the same complaint into the open, where everyone can hear it.

revile vs. decry: Revile goes further than decry: the critic who decries a policy attacks the policy, while the one who reviles it heaps loathing on it — and often on whoever wrote it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-: down

Root — cry: to shout, to call out

Put it together: De- (down) + cry (to shout, from Old French crier) = to cry down. A practice that is decried is shouted down in public — the word has kept the volume of its parts: criticism you can hear across the square.

Use the root in a new word: outcry: News of the stadium's demolition was met with a public outcry that filled three council meetings.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / journalistic

Decry is the press-conference word for criticizing openly — groups decry policies, practices, and trends, at volume and in public. Its unit-mate denounce swings harder: to decry a rule is to keep up the cry against it; to denounce it is to pass official public judgment on it, often in a single thunderclap of a statement. For quiet, sorrowing disapproval, bemoan is nearer the mark.
